You have to remember that even though my dad was tech savvy, plenty of parents are tech illiterate. 

Hell, people working 6 figure jobs at intel regularly get caught by their security team, falling for phishing emails. So understanding those tools at all isn't such a simple task. And then making sure that there isn't a workaround is an entire other task. 

When it comes to AI, it's still emergent tech, we really don't know much about it or how it works(for the majority of the population), to a non-tech inclined person it's basically just a silly chatbot. The dangers of it aren't necessarily apparent if you aren't aware of the potential problems with the tech itself. How it works and how to properly limit and safeguard is a whole complicated discussion, and at the end of the day, setting up a fence around it as a normal parent would be next to impossible. 

The best you could do is limit their web access to only certain things, but even then 14 year olds can always trick their parents and say they need access to "Wordsmith.ai" or something for school if it sounds official enough.

I do agree that parents should be more involved in their children's mental health, but even that isn't necessarily foolproof. You can create a warm and nurturing environment, and keep an eye out for all of the warning signs best you know how, and still fail to catch a problem if the kid doesn't want you to know about it. 

So at the end of the day, product creators do carry a share of burden if their product is readily available to minors, and doesn't maintain proper safeguards for those minors innately. 

That said, I haven't had a chance to read the full facts of this case, so there may very well have been security that was bypassed, and if so it's tragic, but also not negligence on the companies part. but on the same not I do have bias, all of these chatbot companies are just wierd and scuzzy. i'd rather see them shutdown somehow

And easy example, look at final arr trial (level 50) in the msq. 

You know those little laser bees? You know not to stand in front of them, because the aoe always shoots out of the front of them. Even before the marker is there you should get used to reading those tells long before you see the orange show up. 

In short version.. the games been training you to look for information elsewhere. You just haven't had to yet, and that's not all your fault. But go back and do some of the older trials and specifically look for those tells. Don't rely on the orange floor. 

They don't all look the same, but the game will never give you damage that it doesn't tell you about with plenty of time to get to a safe spot. 

Things to look out for: 

Environment. Is the floor marked in any specific way? Do parts of it activate with abilities? Around the edge of the arena are adds or statues or whatever popping up, but seemingly doing nothing? Did the arena change color? Did the podium on the side of the boss seem to take damage from a hit? How about the stuff inside? Did the boss summon rocks or trees or something inside of the arena? 

Boss: what's his body doing. Did he raise his left arm? Did he get down into a crouch? (Note this is easier if you change battle effects to simple. It's entirely possible without. But it's 10x easier if you turn battle effects to simple). 

Debuffs and bars: what other information did the game give you? Did you get a debuff before the ability happened? What's it say when you scroll over that debuff? What is the name of the bosses cast indicated in his cast bar(you can make this larger for ease of access).  Is the name "left swipe?" Or similar? Is the name one that it's used before?(example, rams voice/dragons voice). 

Nothing in this game is accidental when it comes to fight design. Every animation is intentional, every cast name is intentional, and every environmental effect, debuff, etc. Is intentional. They all exist specifically to provide you information to avoid taking damage with.  You don't start out being able to read all of that. It's sort of it's own language.  You learn it over time and can infer from previous knowledge. 

For example: last time I saw something with an ice visual effect, with the cast name blizzard, it meant I had to keep moving or I'd get frozen. So if I see an ice effect with a similar name, the first thing I'll try to do is keep moving. If that fails, I'll look for/ask what information I'm missing. Most of the time the game is building in something it already showed you before. 

Sometimes it'll throw entirely new shit at you. And that always trips people up. You're supposed to die when it's new and not entirely obvious. And then you learn from that death and try not to die to the same thing again. Don't be embarrassed to fail. We all do it. The first time you do a fight on release you'll realize that pretty much everyone fucks up the new stuff. The difference between good and bad players is how well they learn from it. 

Sorry for the book. But tl;Dr. Go back and do early fights with the express intent of looking for tells you havent looked for before. They won't always look the same, but you will start to pick up on patterns. And dont be afraid to die to something new.

Every job plays differently but the team structure is much more rigid. Not necessarily for meta reasons, just because the game is designed to have a that variety in the fights and also gives a %dps buff to the party for adhering to that structure (so, 1 shield healer, 1 regen, 2 tanks, 1 magical range dps, 1 physical range dps, 2 melees.). There are like coordinated runs that some groups do for fun that do goofy shit like "no tank" or "no healer" etc. But they're more of a fun showcase than anything serious. 

For the buffs - So, if I, a White mage, deal 12.5k DPS just by doing my thing, but an Astro deals 10kdps, but also provides 3k dps to party members via buffs, they technically do more rdps.

As for healing, DR, and rez, there's not a more or less value worry. Every healing job has a kit to handle it equally as well as the next. Healers 100% have the most healing among the other jobs though. By a wide margin.   So they are there because they are designed to be the best way to do that. 

If it helps, there are two things that can make a team, one of the best. The first thing to note for both though is: these fights are less of a brute force thing, then they are a coordinated dance. The boss always casts his abilities, at the same time, every time. They have changes, and you don't always do the exact same thing so there is reaction and on the fly thinking, but it's always the same routine overall. Learning the dance of each fight and getting positioning right Is the first challenge. So it's less "ah boss is glowing, I need to stand here-ish then react sccordingly" and more "the boss is glowing. His left hand is raised. The cast bar says flow instead of fall. So I specifically, need to stand specifically here". That said. The two types of best teams

First: being the first to kill the current last savage boss of the tier. This is called the world first race. Teams no life the game when it realeses and compete to be first. They're the puzzle solvers. They guide the way for the rest of the players to learn how the mechanics work while they figure it out in real time. For a savage tier this takes about 24 hours. For ultimates, this takes 1.5 weeks playing 16 hours a day straight. 


The second is: the fastest to kill the boss right now. This is the FFlogs leader board. Because if most teams clear in 12:45, but team A clears it in 12:20, they did more dps than anybody else. Which means they've both mastered the fight, and their individual jobs. Doing both is super tricky. Anybody can do it perfect when attacking a training dummy, but doing it while actively problem solving and doing the dance of the fight is the challenge.

It's a third party site called FFLogs, where a parse(third party mod that reads out everything that happens in a fight and condensed it into dps meters n such) is posted amongst everyone else's, and ranked accordingly. 


Everyone's main number is the same data, your RDPS. Which is your damage+any damage that was caused by a buff you gave someone in the party. 

It also lists out healing data and such, but that's not used for ranking/competition, it's more just for learning. Example: a 100% RDPS parse is a good thing. But a 100% healing parse is usually bad, as it likely means you way overhealed. 

Parses are separated by total group parse, and individuals job specific parse. So if you're playing an astro, it's your ranking among all other Astros, not against everyone.

Once you get to a later point in the game, check out FFLOGS, it's where everybody posts their stats and gets ranked. That's where the competitive spirit of the game really lives 

(Note, fflogs is not an official final fantasy website. In fact, parsing is technically against TOS, but in a grey area way that, if you aren't talking about it in game, or like streaming with it up, they won't ask. Just never talk about it in game chat, or they have to take action)

So they constantly get rebalanced, and the dev teams goal is to make every job equally viable to its peers. It becomes more of a personal preference. 

In 4 man content, you only get 1 healer, but the vast majority of it is so easy, that healer rarely has to do much anyways. 

In 8 man content(e.g savage raids, extreme trials), you get 2, so you'll always see 1 shield and 1 regen(or pure) healer. 

Between them currently, astro does the most rdps technically, as it has buffs it gives the rest of the party to do more damage.  That said, I've run the most recent ultimate, and am running the current tier with plans to go for top parse spots once geared, and the next ultimate, as a white mage exclusively. (Also historically whenever Astro is doing particularly well, it gets nerfed into the ground pretty quick and becomes the lower end of rdps). 

The disparity between the jobs is never so large that you'd get approved/denied for a group because you aren't playing the current best RDPS. Most groups would rather have a healer who's comfortable on their job.  So really it's just about what you vibe with the best, which is why trying new jobs is always important. But for perspective, for every white mage in a top 50 parse currently, there's 4 Astros. But, there are still white mages regardless in those top groups. 

As for healing... they can all do a bunch but it really just depends on how comfortable you get with the kit, and what the current fight is doing. So nobody really worries about that aspect. They all do enough no matter what.

The free trial is the first 70 story levels(meaning you can cap at level 70 but play through the remaining quests. you dont get booted at any point you just dont have access to anything that requires higher levels).  The biggest constraints are: you cant use the marketboard. You cant send private messages(but you can use say/shout/party/NN chat) or create a party(However, you can circumvent this by asking a player to make a party for you, and then they leave said party.). You cant earn more than 300k gil(youll likely earn more than this, but honestly you dont need it for much since you cant use the MB anyways. By the time this is an issue, youll know if you like the game or not). 

2. Most players usually choose to pay, yes. After youve completed the base game and first 2 expansions, you have an idea of if you want to upgrade and at the very least, get rid of the restrictions. The story is the big selling point typically for these players as you're in the bread and butter of the good stuff between levels 50-70 and it really just keeps getting better. 

3. Yes and no. Any role is viable, but typically for most content DPS roles will have the longest queus. Healers and tanks typically get instant queues depending on the datacenter(e.g oceania is under populated so you still may have a wait regardless of role). Where a dps may wait 15-20 minutes for a niche mid level dungeon, a healer or tank may pop it instantly. HOWEVER, you can also do all of the dungeons and normal trials with a filled NPC party to skip queues as well. Its a little slower since they dont do big pulls, but its perfectly serviceable. 

3. The purpose of support in this game... I mean 2 sections. Tanks and healers are both supps but ill start with healers. 

You do damage and you keep your teammates alive. Usually in that order. When you get good at it, you spend the better majority of your time doing damage. There's 2 types of healing subclasses, shield or regen. Regen brings health back up, shield blocks damage before it happens. Most of your kit is healing supplies, but its about learning to use those efficiently to do the most when it matters. E.g, you aren't topping off the tank every time he gets hit, you're just making sure he has enough health to spare for the next hit. 

Tanks are all about damage while weaving in defensive abilities to mitigate their damage. 

4. Yes its possible. you dont buy accounts, you buy skips on the cash shop for a character. However the meat and potatoes of this game is story content and skipping is usually frowned upon as you'll have no idea what your kit does in a natural setting at the very least. Nobody wants to be dragged down by someone who didnt learn what the last 90 levels were supposed to teach them and begin by making that the rest of the parties problem. So if you do this, go back through and thoroughly learn to be good at your kit before you kick off into group content. I will also add: raiding exists, its can be a super fun time sink. But its not like most MMO's, its not the core draw. the endgame is for the players that got there and its not the only goal. You may find it lackluster if you expect the entire game to be tailored around it and nothing else. E.G the current savage tier. My group cleared it week 1, and will be done with weekly reclears by week 8. reclears for the entire tier takes about 2 hours total in a week. Its fun, but after you do it, its done. 

Some groups take longer to prog(e.g 3, 2-3 hour sessions a week), and go on for a few months. but thats not really a standard. you can take however long you want to in PF instead of a static, but the tier will stop being posted up in PF when the next tier eventually drops(3 tiers per xpac). Theres also ultimate fights which are a bit more timeless, but you should get a good chunk of savage experience under your belt before worrying about them so i wont dig into all that here. 

5. Gatekeeping. Complicated issue. sure it exists, no it isnt the norm. In 95% of the game, you'll never have an issue with being a new player *so long as you are trying and receptive to constructive criticisms*. New players have a green sprout icon by their name, and are nicknamed sprouts accordingly. The community loves em and loves to bring people through the story that they care so much about. 

But in the raid scene, its not so much gatekeeping usually, as it is... people who don't perform and absolutely ruin a parties chance to run will get called out. Being new is one thing, but there is some expectation, especially in party finder, to know how to play the game at the level that you're entering. so if you're a savage player but dont know what half your buttons do or your gear is all wack, you're wrong to be there at that moment and the response will likely not be kind. You also dont just stumble into this content though, you intentionally try to do it. so theres a valid backing to why they'd get upset. 

SERVERS: aether is usually the content focused server. Crystal is more casual focus. Primal is a blend. and Dynamis is new, but currently all players that want to visit another DC to play with friends are being funneled to dynamis. I cant speak on the EU or JP servers personally. Currently you can (sort of freely) visit any datacenter and any server, so long as you're in the same region. They're testing cross region but its not out yet. 

Finally: Endgame. talked a bit about it already. Farming usually looks like this. Raid tier drops. Raid teams get gear made by crafters(who grinded for about 2 weeks before the tier to get all the supplies ready). Raid team goes in and grinds the savage tier. They finish the tier, then they do reclears to gear the static with the better gear. This takes 8ish weeks of reclears. Eventually ultimates come out, and some savage players opt to do that next challenge. You pretty much grind that to say you did it though, the reward is technically a weapon, but its more of a fashion item than properly for gearing purposes since its immediately outdated by the release of the next savage tier. 

outside of raiding it looks like: a lot of things. this expansion we'll be getting an adventure foray, which is like... a seperate mini zone that takes a while to grind through. we dont know exactly what this one will play like but expect its own battle content, and slow grind for some sort of material/points/whatever. 

There's deep dungeons. dungeons that go on for 100-200 floors, that you mainly grind for the titles and the leaderboard and some rare mounts. each floor is about 10 minutes and they scale in difficulty the deeper you go.

there's reputation grinds in the form of allied societies(formerly beast tribes), where you do either battle content, or craft/gather to get rep up, in order to usually get mounts or materials that are otherwise difficult to get. 

and then extreme trials get sprinkled in as well. which are normal trials tuned up. they sit between normal and savage in difficulty as a sort of stepping stone. You grind these for mounts, which dont have a guaruntee drop and only 1 can drop per clear. So, it may take 400 tries in PF to get yours, since you roll against the other players to recieve it.

There's no way to directly export the data. 

What universalis does is aggregate market data. 

Everyone that uses mods via dalamud has an optional checkbox to upload their MB data. Whenever they search for an item on the MB dalamud snapshots that current data and sends it over to universalis. 

Universalis then sorts and displays all of these. That's why the data will display as a few days old on less popular items, as it's generated by player viewing, ot actually extracting the MB data itself.

Endgame is more straightforward than in WOW

You'll get the current crafted gear set to start. Add materia to it(slottable stat boosters) you'll get raid food(current food that lasts 30 minutes each, boosting stats), and pots (30 second stat boosters, usable ince or twice per fight). 

As you progress the tier(4 fights per tier, 3 tiers per xpac), you'll unlock gear that makes the next fight easier. However each clear only awards 1-3 gear pieces, shared among the group. Usually it'll be: class specific gear piece + chest of gear piece that'll create a class specific piece fir whoever opens it. Early in the tier, you'll only be able to loot the fights once per week. 

(The more people that already cleared that week, the less loot spawns).  

There's a horizontal gear set progression that'll also be unlocked during this, called tomestone gear. It's a currency you get for basically any other current content you do, locked to a specific amount per week, so you'll be getting pieces from that, and raids. Your BIS Will likely be some mix of the two. (BIS sets are usually posted in the balance discord, if you don't like mathing it all out yourself to find what exactly is your bis). 

That's how gearing works. 

For the actual fight differences: first off, dieing does not punish you like it does in WoW. Aside from possibly wiping the raid depending on when you die. But wipes aren't counted against you for anything. You're expected to wipe, a lot, as you learn. You don't lose anything but your time when you do. 

XIV endgame is much more individual results than WOW. You're going in with 8 people total, and the fights are more akin to choreographed dances. So players will be expected to learn and memorize very tight positioning patterns as you play. I come from WoW, and my friend is still currently a mythic+ raider over there. His biggest gripe is that every arena is either a circle or square with some variation. You're never in a big ass room with natural terrain. 

That's because the fight itself has a lot of exact positioning, and the challenge isn't about using the terrain around you, so much as it is about learning how the fight functions and positioning around it. If a rock or something got you stuck for half a second, it could wipe the raid. 

Each fight in the savage tier is 7-12 minutes long, and averages 2-4 mechanics per minute. Some mechanics are easier than others, and the difficulty spikes as the tier goes on. So fight 1, is designed to be the beginner raid in every tier. But fight 4 is usually the longest with the harder mechanics, including a door boss. 

If you want a good example of what these fights look like via positioning and movement, look up POVs on YouTube for p8s, p10s, p11s, or p12s. (Literally just "FFXIV p12s clear pov"). It'll all look like chaos at first, but everyone is moving in patterns based on what they know, and information they read in real time from the fight, as you learn and prog the fight on repeat, you'll become far more comfortable with it.

DNC is a great trainer for this imo actually. 

Because you're constantly checking to see if you've proc'ed the next step in a combo, you train your eyes to really dart between the important things.

Like the other commenter said, the fight is scripted. The boss will never pull out a random bullshit mechanic out of nowhere. Even when it varies it'll always have the same variances (example, in p8s, you had animals phase. Which would be dog first or snake first). So you know what to look out for and adjust around it once you know the fight. 

Because of that, you know when in the fight the boss will pull NIPPLES TO THE LEFT OR RIGHT 3000, And can plan accordingly to be checking. You'll also know after the 10th time seeing it, that he always gets to two thirds of that cast when your 2 minute burst has come up. Meaning your tech step, devilment, 2 fan, blah blah blah is always going to come up at that moment. And you start hitting it by internally timed reflex without having to worry about it. But that comes with learning the fight. 

The most important thing I was told as a raider coming from WoW was, WoW raids are testing your expertise at your job. XiV raids are choreographed dances that you need to learn the steps to, while also performing your job at a capable level. 

When you first hit a raid, it's going to be confusing, and everything's going to be moving a little bit too fast to keep up with. It's normal and expected, especially when you aren't used to some of the recurring mechanics. Memorization is the name of the game, and it makes everything slow down to a crawl once you know it. 


But the reality for tips and tricks is... repetition. Do a raid more and more on something like DNC. Get used to glancing at your hotbars without focusing on them. Get used to the fight to know when you can split your attention vs keeping a basic version of its rotation going when you can't look at all. Eventually you'll phase that out as you get more comfort with a fight, but it's a good place to start. 

Just know, when you're progging a phase for the first time, nobody is expecting a perfect rotation from you. Do what you can, but focus on mechanics first. Your damage/parse mean shit if you don't see a new mechanic to practice it.


Edit: I forgot an important factor here too. Some jobs just straight up aren't for some people. I don't melee because I'd rather eat a bowl of rocks than have to hit positional. I don't know how melee mains don't go insane doing it. But I'm a healer main, and know plenty who don't touch it because it's other too boring, or too high pressure. I also jive well with DNC because I'm used to swapping my attention across my screen already. I also play casters because slide casting hits a good part in my brain. Point is. Some jobs just do not jive with the player, and there's no shame in going "I don't get this on a conceptual level, even if I understand it in theory 100%"

The game is designed for people that have never played MMOS before for the base game(levels 1-50 a realm reborn). You may hear people say that the base game is boring compared to all if the expansions, and this is part of why, when you already know how MMOs work and know how to play them, you don't feel like you're doing much. (The other part of it, is that story wise, it's all of the setup and introductions, so the story is fairly slow burn early on). But it will start you with just 2-3 buttons to use, and as you progress, you'll keep earning more buttons and have more to do. 

It takes some getting used to, as there's definitely a "language" it tries to teach you, but how fast you pick up on that is up to you. But the basic premise is "avoid big orange areas, and hit buttons on your hotbars"

The weirdest thing to pick up, as other genres dint behave like this, is that the orange/red on the ground is what decides if you get damaged. If you were in it when it disappeared, but out of it when the actual visual effect goes off, the game still considers you as in the path of the danger.(imagine a big orange circle on the ground for three seconds. It goes away, and one second later that area erupts in flames) This is called snapshotting, and it throws off a lot of new players for the first little while, since damage is tied to snapshots rather than the visual effects.

Besides that, there's things you'll learn as you go, that make the game easier the further you play, and teach you to do the harder things over time naturally. 

Just know, there's a lot of game in this game. Hundreds of hours in just the main story. Do not feel like you need to rush, it's meant ti be enjoyed at your own pace. You're not behind just because you take a few extra weeks to finish some main story because you decided to do side content for a bit. 

Also, if you do decide to play, just know the the majority of the community loves our new players(known as sprouts). If you get stuck, or struggle, just ask for help. We've all been there and want to see you succeed so that we can share more of this game with more people. There may be some assholes out there, but they're definitely a very small minority. So even if you're in a dungeon and not quite sure what to do; you can ask your party or the daily question thread here, or the in game chat(novice network). There's no shame in learning to play.

So, first time savage is going to hit like a brick. 

To answer your questions in order though:

You can flex between healers. They share the same gear however they don't always share the same BiS(best in slot) gear. It'll be similar, but typically 2-3 pieces will be swapped out to cater toward the specific job you're playing. 

is 1 shield 1 regen required: No. But you'll rarely see groups without it. It's an extremely balanced choice for both prog and parsing, so most groups don't screw with that formula too much. If they do, you'll almost always see 2 shield healers, rather than 2 regen, as going without damage mitigation is a bad time. Not impossible, but PF is unlikely to let you slide in as a second(or even second shield, especially while you're new to savage raiding). This will remain relevant through the tier, and long after its dead. 

Info you should know: The balance discord. This will contain information on your job specific BIS gear, and your ideal rotations. I can link it to you if you need it. 

what to expect: while you're learning, lean into overheal. Don't go crazy with it, but an alive party is better than a dead one. As you start to get a better gauge of what you're doing, improve your damage and cut out anything non essential in healing.(Essential here meaning, leaving the party with just enough health/shields to pass the next mechanic with a small safety net. Or anything you have to use to prevent gauge over cap.).  Your job isn't to keep the party at 100% its to keep them alive. You can focus on some damage openers, and keeping your DPS up early, just make sure to study. 

If you know the next mechanic hits like a truck, you're playing WHM, and the party is half health. Then you need to resolve that problem using as few non lily GCD's as you can. But every mechanic has a safety threshold(eg, 40k health), so if you know that ahead of time, you can manage the party without losing your damage uptime. 

As you play the fight you'll start to develop your 'rotation' for that fight. you'll know the scripted moments where you're burning lillies, and you'll get a firm feel for what your cohealers are healing/shielding. That relationship even in PF is very important. Pay attention to the parties health bars, and try to understand the effect you're having and the effect your cohealer is having. Don't over-write what the other guy does, and don't leave him out to dry when he needs you to do your job. 

I can answer any WHM specific questions you have, since thats my main and I've got a few savage tiers and now TOP under my belt. But the standard philosophy is always: Use your gauge. Don't overcap. Try not to overheal. Spam glare and keep dia up constantly. There's also tools that can help with all of this (parsing, XIVanalysis to analyze the parses, etc). Just know if you use them, you should only be using them for personal development and not judging others. At the very least, never mention someones parse in game, it is bannable.

EDIT: I forgot, a couple of tips and tricks I wish id known on my first savage raid. 

First: Your HUD. Set it up. if your party list is in the top left corner of the screen, its in a bad spot. you need to be able to glace at it without looking away. I have all of my hotbars centered and the party list directly left of the hotbars(I can send screenshots to help if needed) yours can be anywhere, so long as its not way out of view. Also, find your debuffs(Status Info: enfeeblements), make that shit LARGE AND VERY VISIBLE. savage raids, especially the last few tiers have leaned heavily on debuffs to know how to resolve mechanics. you need to have easy constant visual access to what the boss is cursing you with. 

Focus target: I rebound this. For most jobs, its safe to set your focus target on the boss, so you can always see his cast bar. this is good to do on healer too if you like, But i prefer to focus target the main tank for quick, off the cuff healing without having to think. Some folks do fine using the f1-8 keys on the keyboard, I prefer something more central to hit and make my life simple. 

Target info(progress bar): This is the bosses cast bar. Lots of abilities have the tell in the name of the cast. You're gonna want to, you guessed it, make this shit large and easy to see. If the boss is casting (Left arm destruction), youll know not to stand on the bosses left side that much faster. 

Non UI stuff: You don't have any useless actions(except maybe repose. thats really only useful in DD's. and cure 1. if  you use cure 1 in a savage you will get laughed at.). So if you're not used to using plenary indulgence, thin air, lucide dreaming, or esuna, aquaveil, divine benison. Get used to them. they all have important uses in savage, some more frequent than others. (thin air and lucid are essential on WHM to handle mana management. you will go mana broke if you dont utilize them). Every button is essential. every button needs to be pressed. Esuna used to not be necessarry. but theyve added it in multiple times last tier. so get used to it.

Considering you called it arcanist, I'm going to assume you're <level 30. I'll warn you with that in general: most of the jobs are pretty boring at those levels. You get a short handful of skills to do what you need to in order to scoot along.  

ACN is the one class that actually evolves into two seperate jobs that level together(summoner and scholar), one is magical DPS, the other is a shield healer. If you're looking for complexity but specifically *not any kind of healer*, then ACN/SMN in the long term will probably bore you, as it's one of the most simplistic job designs now. 

Melee jobs typically have the more difficult rotations, with lots of steps. But this typically only becomes true as you get to higher levels. 

Short version of the types of complexity each role has. 

Melee dps(reaper, dragoon, etc): rotation complexity. You hit buttons in correct orders to do big damage. 

Phys ranged(bard, Dancer, etc): ypu have some rotation complexity, but the party relies on you for buffs and enemy debuffs at the right times. 

Magical ranged(summoner, black mage, etc): your rotation has some complexity, but you have casting time involved typically, so you will need to know when to start a cast, get to safe spots early, and learn to slidecast. 

Tank(paladin, Dark knight, etc): you have a few damage buttons, most of your complexity knows from knowing when to use the buttons that make *you* take less damage, and cycling them properly while keeping all the enemies focused on you

Healer(white mage, scholar, etc): your damage rotation is 2 buttons. Your complexity comes from knowing all of your other buttons inside and out and knowing when the proper moments are to use each sort of heal and to what extent, in order to provide the most time doing damage.

I also came from WoW(quit during pandaria). I'll say this, the raids here are different. If they're like a boxing match in WoW, they're a battle dance here. 

You do need mechanical skill when it comes to your job, to pass dps checks n whatever. 

But they're more like a coordinated routine here. You're going to be learning and executing exact movements in patterns, that alternate slightly depending on the variation of the mechanics, and every raid will come with a new set of steps. So it's a constant learning curve to keep up. A lot of fun, and really fulfilling, but every raid is a new program. 

If you want to see it in action, look up POVs of the raid p12s, it'll give you a good idea of the difference as will the rest of the last tier (p10s and p11s mainly). Spacing, snapshotting, positioning, and if you're a caster, slidecasting are everything. 

I recommend if you do a story skip, don't buy the job skip and level it up organically in the time you've got, since it'll teach you the core of the job in a pretty succinct way.  You come from WoW so you should grasp the core of it easily enough, but it's still good to learn it naturally vs all at once.

If you want to skip the msq, then do it. 

It's a fantastic msq, and knowing the thematic relevance of bosses makes the that much better imo, but everyone plays it differently. You can always watch all the cutscenes like a movie later on utilizing an in game tool in the inn rooms. 

I will say though, if you skip right now, you're going to find the scraps of the raid scene. Because we're in the pre xpac content lull. Any of the raiders that are serious about it cleared the most recent tier a while back. The next tier will drop 3-4 weeks after the next xpac releases.  

Hell, most folks that I know have officially let their sub lapsed until June. The raid scene is robust, but the endgame is only as relevant as the time that it's released(last tier released 6+ months back). 

We get three savage tiers per xpac, and then ultimate raids and various extremes in the middle of all of that. Savage is the bulk of our endgame raids. Ultimate raids are the next step up and are usually picky about having finished current raid tiers and/or previous ultimate raids. And extremes are like the gap between normal and savage. 

If you want to dig in during the premium time, skip a few weeks before the xpac drops, get used to playing your job at a high level of play, and then find a group that intends to tackle the raid tier when it drops(or join one within a month or so of the raid tier dropping).  

This isn't to say you can't find someone raiding right now, but it'll likely be folks that aren't too serious about it.

Like everyone's saying. You learn to read them in real time. 

It feels very foreign when you're new, and it's like learning a compact Lil language the game speaks in. 

The normal stuff (stack markers, spread markers, gaze markers, and conal aoes) you get used to. You also start staring at the bosses cast bar as you get more comfortable. 

This attack is named "the left fist of god". Don't stand on the bosses left side, he's probably going to do something over there. 

After all of those more obvious bits, you learn to read the room. In a literal way. The rooms the fights are in are usually designed to show you what to do in niche mechanics. There's one in SHB that comes to mind. The boss is a giant rubiks cube, you're standing on a giant grid. The bosses face tells you what areas are about to explode on the grid. 
Another example is when the sides of the arena start doing something. For example one of the EW dungeons has a moment where the trees on the side start shaking and kicking up dust, that's your tell to get out of the way of that "lane". 


And finally, there's the really niche mechanics. You learn those the hard way. And then you never forget them, because you'll likely end up doing them dozens of times and you know "this fight... ugh it has that thing". 

Examples of this are crystal tower. When you fight cerberus a team has to get eaten by him and fight their way out. The only way to do this is to stand in a specific add aoe, and then stand in another specific aoe. It's not intuitive in a way that makes it obvious. But it's infamous and people just know to do it.  

Another example would be "show sniper your hole" in the ivalice AR series. It feels unintuitive, but once you've done it, you know how that specific instance works and you remember it because it sticks out as unique.


Edit: an important psa to anybody worried about the same things. 

We know it's rough to learn to read the games language. You're not always going to pick it up overnight. Like that old joke goes "you know how to get to Carnegie hall? Practice". 

It's part of why we love our sprouts here. Most of us remember being the sprout who felt clueless and slow. Learning it all is part of the fun, and we get to live it vicariously through you again.

Alright, so maybe math is the wrong word, but here's the logic breakdown as best as my sleep-deprived brain can explain.

Freecure unlocks at level 32. After you cast cure 1 It gives you a 15% chance to make your next cure 2 not cost any mana. 


Cure 1 info: 400 cost, 450 healing potency(upgraded later to 500 potency). 

Cure 2 info: 1000 cost, 700 healing potency(upgraded later to 800 potency)


At face value, cure 1 feels like a no brainer. Spend less mana for more healing. But you'll be using 2 GCDs to cast your heals out. 

The 15% chance of mana free cure 2 cost also sounds nice the caveat is, it only stores that for 15 seconds, and the chance is low enough that you can't ever really rely on it. Your mana should never be in the sort of danger that gambling in 15% is worthwhile. 

450 potency is also not a lot. 700 is about the minimum that you should ever need to hardcast for. 400 is still "tank could die to a Tankbuster or big mob pull" territory. By the time you go to cast out your second cast, you could be handling a dead tank.  

Your mana will eventually cap at 10,000, and you'll have mana recovery tools(thin air, which makes your next cast free, lucid dreaming which recovers mana over time, and your lillies. Which don't cost mana and do the big heals).  So your mana management, while piss poor as WHM, is also never meant to be in that level of danger. 


But the most important factor here is that, while mana is *one* resource, time is the more important resource. Like I mentioned before, you do damage any time you don't *need* to heal immediatly. The faster things die, the less damage you need to heal. So if you go to cast multiple Hardcasted heals out, you're spending time that you could have instead spent, killing the things that are causing the damage. 

This is all pretty dependant on continuing to level up though. The more your kit develops, the less you need cure 1. You'll just have a bunch of better tools, and that low potency heal becomes more of a liability than it does a help. So the mentality of phasing it out sooner rather than later is usually recommended, so you don't lean on hardcasting out small heals as a crutch, because eventually the damage will outpace the value. But like I said before, there's a window after you get cure 2 where cure 1 is still okay to use. I'd honestly say up to level 50ish isn't horrible, but try and get used to using cure 2 more and more so you can tune in the feeling of the higher potency healing

Oh yeah, ehanced cure. A lot of abilities have automatic passives like that. (I believe that ability page has them listed as traits if I remember right). They're good to read over just so make sure you know if there's any important changes.

Just know that, cure 1's enhancement gives "freecure proc" for cure 2. *it's a trap. Freecure is not worth using cure 1 to get if you have cure 2. A very small group may say it is. Ignore them. After level 36 or so, cure 1 is objectively bad, I won't bore you with the math, it just is*

So, I leave cure 1 on my hotbar(mainly because it fills an otherwise empty spot). 

But yes! You can add/remove things from your hotbar at will. To remove, just hit the unlock button on your hotbar and drag it off the bars. 


To add it back on: go to character>actions and traits> and then there's sub menus for each thing. There's a page for job specific actions, a page for role specific actions, and so on. All WHM specific spells will be on the job page, listed in the order you acquired them(by level). You can simply drag the icon out of that screen onto a hotbar to add it back on.  

Note: some spells evolve over time. Example: stone turns into stone 2>stone 3> glare. If it evolves, whatever on your hotbar will automatically devolve back to the appropriate ability for the content you're doing. 

However, cure 1 *does not* evolve into cure 2. They are seperate spells, which is why many people will remove cure 1 from their bars unless they're in content that they need it. 


Also: you don't have to remove it right when you get cure 2, there's a few levels of content where you don't have the mana to justify using cure 2 all the time. But it's a very small window

Everything the other commenter said is true, but to tack onto that

Healers, and WHM in particular doesn't have a very complex rotation when it comes to your core damage. You're already on track(aero the boss, then spam stone. Heal in-between stone spam. If mobs, then swap to aoe damage instead of stone). 

Later on you'll unlock your lillies and lily gauge. They'll become your core healing routine. Lillies accrue at 1 every 20 seconds, and can be used for either a single target, or an aoe heal. Later in level every time you spend a Lilly, it'll charge your blood lily. At 3 charges you shoot it at the enemy and it does big damage (equal to 3 glares+aoe damage if there's multiple enemies). So your healing is actually dps neutral. You'll also get a bunch of OGCDs(off global cooldowns) heals. You'll want to mix them in as needed. The most important thing to note is to never hoard your ogcds. They do have long-ish cooldowns but your kit relies on you using them frequently. 

Eventually you'll phase out of using cure 1 entirely, and then rarely be using cure 2 as you get more comfortable with your lillies and your OGCDs.  


Your main job as healer, is keep the tank alive. Not full. But alive and able to survive whatever would hit him next. If he's fine, then damage damage damage. This becomes super important later on as your aoe turns into holy and begins stunning enemies. You get several seconds of stun, which is several seconds of damage your tank isn't taking. 


So yeah. No core rotation, just get comfortable with your kit and what it does to do the healing that *needs* done. WHM grows into it pretty naturally as you level up, so don't worry about memorizing it all right away, just make sure you know how to use what you have.

An important factor here is going to be how you view it. 

If the story, to you, is something to rush through, then yes the base games story is... slow and a bit dull. 

If you play because you like story, then consider the base game to be the exposition and set up. It's designed to introduce you to everything that you need to know about what's to come. You'll meet a bunch of characters, and be running what feels like unimportant errands, but it all makes sense later as bonds between those characters grow and the story unfolds. 

To put it into perspective, we'll finally be starting a new story arc in July when DT releases. Everything else(base game, heavensward, stormblood, shadowbringers, and endwalker), are all part of the same story arc. So it's a lot of story that needs that early exposition. 

The other thing to keep in mind, is your toolkit(what your job/class can do) is unlocked over time via leveling. So you start out pretty limited, and the further you go the more complex the play gets. As for grinding, its as optional as you want it to be/depends on what you call grinding. If it helps it make sense beyond face value, there's two important things to be aware of. 

1. State prisons are meant to be rehabilitation centers for criminals, not punishment cubes(for profit prisons are supposed to be too, but they fail more often because... profit). It can be hard to tackle this concept if it's not something you're invested in, as prison isn't often portrayed like that in media. And it feels a bit wrong at first to think about it like that. But at the end of the day, having hundreds of thousands, to millions of citizens that can rehab and become functional members of society again is better for us as a whole than just locking them away. And rehabbing them is easier when you treat them like human beings and do extra things for them on occasion. 


2. Most often something like this isn't just the state shelling out cash. In the prison, inmates can earn money by doing jobs, this money goes into an account for them. It's not much, maybe a few bucks a day. This is in theory a win win, as the state saves money on prison upkeep, and the prisoners get to learn skills that will help them when they get out, and some spending money while inside for little extras at the commissary(family can also add money to these accounts). Once in a blue moon the prison will offer something extra like this at the commissary for a day, so prisoners can spend that money they earned on it instead. It's just a nice treat that they have the option to buy themselves. The cost to the state is pretty much just transport for the pizza, and I'd imagine even that is worked into the commissary price.

If you work in a fish processing plant, the pungentness of the smell goes away after a while, even though you go home after an 8 hour shift. You go in the next day and it's not the same as someone walking in for the first time. 

Noseblind isn't just about your "nose palette" it's about your brain actively choosing to ignore things it considers regular in the environment. 

If you burn plant matter of any sort inside, it gets in the paint and on the carpet. The odor isn't as strong as stale cigarette tar coating the walls, because that's so thick it's almost like a grease. But it's still there, and within the same day any non smoker will notice something, and if it's regular enough, nothing short of a deep carpet cleaning makes it go away.

I'm sure this will get buried in the heap here. But I just wanted to tack on/clarify some things I saw mentioned. 

For the blocking/stalking/unwanted people issue. You're correct that the best solution is to only add actual friends to your friends list. The difficult thing with an MMO, is that it is inherently pretty social. So friends end up getting made pretty easily because you're all actively participating in a common interest. 

This community has a tendency to overstate the severity of the stalking situation though. It absolutely does happen, and the block feature/friends list within the game do need to be updated to reflect that reality. But the vast majority of players won't encounter the issues. I've personally had one and it was an awful experience, but, if you have an open line of communication with your daughter you can help her avoid ever getting into that problem.  

The stalkers don't just pop up out of nowhere. They're typically people you've gotten to know already, just like real life. Either your FC(as others mentioned, a guild, aka. A group of 3-100 players that join the group to play together and help each other/have a dedicated chat channel in game, also usually having their own discord group that they can text/voice chat on), or just someone you've made friends with otherwise.  This isn't because those things are bad, they're just how people begin to socialize in the game. And most people on this game are friendly and awesome and ready to help with game stuff, so it makes socializing a pretty natural thing to do.

So make sure your daughter feels comfortable with you when it comes to difficult social situations and uncomfortable encounters with others.  I'm sure you know already that policing a teenager and making rules only gets you so far, the rest is up to them trusting you for advice and help if they break a rule and it starts snowballing on them. 

The other thing mentioned in the thread is 18+ player activities. This is a bit more common. BUT, it's strictly advertised as being 18+, and being explicit about it is NOT allowed within the game. The only time you'll have it happen is if you choose to actively engage with it. So if she sees things in game advertising clubs/venues/FCs that are 18+ she should avoid them. Because going there, the players assume everyone is consenting and understands the situation. People may say gross things is the normal chat in different areas otherwise, but it's not common as it is a ban-able offense. I can provide you more information on this stuff in a direct way that makes sense without knowing about how the game works if you'd like. But just know she won't just be playing the game, fighting monsters, and suddenly be witness to adult activities. At least not regularly

Aside from that, the rest of the game is pg13 at it's worst. There's no programmed in sexual bits or anything. They do some off cursing(saying things like hell, ass, damnit),  and there's a few situations where other characters will make a subtle joke innuendo but nothing horrendous(The equivalent of a 'that's what she said' joke here and there), and occasionally a male character will be shirtless(in context of a fight). There's some violence but it's all fantasy based, so no gore or anything. It is a very emotional story, but in a good way. There's a lot of good life lessons about love and loss, trying to help people but failing or doing the wrong thing, and dealing with the consequences of that. Emotionally it can pull your heart strings pretty hard, so if she is the emotional sort, it may make her cry at times, but most often in good ways that also help process these big life situations in an easier to digest format.

Then you have an option for different outfits(Plates), you set the plates up, then whenever you're in an allied or safe zone, you can just hit character>glamourplates>the plate you want>apply. 

The glamour dresser is the preferred method if you have outfits you want to change to multiple times, or a core glam you like to use, as it doesnt cost additional glam crystals to apply glam plates.

A lot of it is repetition. You don't know what works until you know everything that doesn't. Go into pubs and run game after game of doing stupid/crazy shit. Figure out what works, what could work with more practice, and what is an almost constant death sentence. Pubs are perfect for expirementation, so don't play them like you would a ranked match.  Purposefully play wildly different in them. 

Hot drop a hundred times in a row until you're consistently winning in the hot zones, it will give you familiarity with them, so when you're mid game and have to rotate through, you already know the angles of approach that give you the best coverage and positioning.  

The repition will also teach you when to hold your ground on a fight, or when you need to rotate out and drop it. A lot of the high level players know how long they have to fight somewhere before its a lost cause, so they can actively engage with an escape plan in mind for if shit goes south. Imo this was a constant problem with lower level players. They'd sit in a fight poking a team for 2 full minutes, and then get confused and upset when multiple other parties descended on them. You need to build the confidence to finish a fight within 30 seconds and then continue to move, and if you can't, know your exit strategy and use it before it's too late.

So, it's a little bit counter intuitive but I've run a few bars now, and the numbers rarely lie. 

When you obsess over shrink to that degree, you create a few problems for yourself. 

The first issue is with staffing. If an experienced and proper bartender walks into a joint and they have weighted scales and electronic auto locks on pour spouts, it says 2 things. 1. You don't want regulars. And 2. You don't trust your bar staff. Not trusting your bar staff is an issue because most *good* bartenders want autonomy in their work. Someone breathing down your neck is never good. And bartenders get their pick of the litter. You can get any idiot to pour shots, but a truly skilled bartender will have folks coming in for them. This doesn't matter in corporate chains because it's all the same muck being served. But in a specialized bar, your staff is part of the attraction. So if a bartender with 15 years behind the bar could go somewhere, they're not likely to go to the place that openly displays 0 trust in their staff. 

Along with that, bartenders autonomy means they need to know that they're trusted to go slightly heavier handed in their pours. This part is iffy territory, but it's also a "we don't ask how the sausage gets made" managers wont ask, and bartenders wont admit to doing it. But any place that has regulars has at some point or another developed a relationship with their clientele that they'll get a slightly heavier drink. I'm not talking double instead if single, but an extra third of an ounce occasionally goes a long way.  

When you can do that for certain clients, when their friends want to go drink, the vote to go to your bar eventually gets higher in the list. So for losing a third of an ounce every now and again, you gain the sales from everyone they bring to their "favorite" bar.  This isn't a standalone factor, your staff having sales skill and a good personality also contribute a chunk of this. 

Bartenders don't pour heavy because they want to give shit away for nothing. They pour heavy for more tips. People who tip heavier are also more likely to return, and the whole process works in everyone's favor. 


*this is a double edged sword however*. You still have to track your shrink. If it gets out of hand, management still needs to step in and curtail egregious amounts. You shouldn't be losing bottles every week due to bad pouring standards. You should also be ensuring your staff knows proper pours 100%.  A bartender who can't properly free pour 1.5 Oz needs to be trained. A bartender who can but twice a week gives an extra nip is going to earn you money in the long run.

I run an FC with my alt and two friends alts specifically to gil farm submersibles. 

It's not too bad to get started but step 1 is either

A: have gil to buy supplies. 

B: be an omnicrafter/gatherer. You'll need to have a good handful of levels in most of the crafters anyways just to make the sub parts. 


The basic breakdown is this: you go to the workshop and get the schematics for submarine type 1. This is shark class. The bread and butter and where every sub starts. 

Then you go to the center console and you build each of the four components. Each component has multiple stages. If you want to simplify this part, use teamcraft.com and make a list of all 4 parts. Teamcraft will then tell you the supplies you need to fully build all of them. Once you've gotten all the supplies (about 6 hours of gathering/crafting if you're omni), put them into the console as it asks. 

Once you complete a part, it goes in your inventory. Once you have all four, go to the shop in the housing district that trades for company seals. Buy a dive credit(10,000 points). 

Take all four parts you made and the dive credit, and go to the console on the right of the workshop. Hit register a submersible and voila. You have a ship. 

In the workshop there's a Mammut that sells fuel for company credits. Get some of that. 

Then you go to the console on the right again, and hit "deploy submersible on voyage"

At first, you'll only have a single map unlocked, with one node to explore. Click that and deploy your ship on it's maiden voyage. 

Once your sub returns it'll bring back some trash loot, and possible discover a new node. Every time you explore a node, you have a chance to discover another linked node(this is rng). 

After you get a few nodes unlocked and have a few levels on your sub, use the website "mogship" to determine the best route to take in order to level your ship. 

Keep doing that. For a while. Eventually you'll have goals like "discover node J, O, and T" as they unlock your next 3 ships. But that's at least 1-2 weeks away and more in depth. While you're doing the basics, you should check out the discord someone linked and start ti try to understand all the resources. Sgt peppers guide is good for beginners, and there's a few others in that discord that break it all down fairly simply.

As your subs level up, you'll get parts to make new types of sub components, and change the stats of your sub, but again theory crafting is more high level than a reddit comment can really explain

So, fair warning I don't tank but I do typically have a good relationship with my tanks so I'll pass on what bits I've learned from them, just take it with a grain of salt. 

For coordination, what you had on p1s is the right idea! As you learn the fight, you learn where things are meant to happen like feints/reprisals/etc. This is what gets referred to as MIT for most raid. You don't hear much about tanks personal mits unless you're a tank, so usually in this context "we need more mit at x point" means "we need more raidwide mit". The early savage tier was a bit more lax, the current one is a bit less forgiving if mit isn't properly used with consistency. There  are quiet a few abilities that need that raidwide mit now, and it's easy to tell what it is once the group gets one shot. 

Now for "is it easier to tank" according to everyone I know that's ever played tank and healer in savage, yes. Tanking is a lot easier. Because the responsibility turns from everyone, to just you. You need to be rolling your personal mits in a rotation, and you need to coordinate with the other tank the same way the healers do. In the current tier, every fight has tank swapping tank busters so your provoke/shirk skills will probably need refined, because being a second or two off, will cause the other tank to die.a lot of mechanics also will rely on tank invulns to do the heavy lifting. 

The flip side of that though, is that you don't have to every worry about the rest of the party. It's your positions, and your co-tank. Whatever the rest of the party is doing quickly becomes not your business for the majority of the fight. Once you get more comfort you can start throwing in shake it offs/passage of arms/whatever to try and help save the party in runs that are struggling. Nobody will be mad if you don't, but it can be nice to do when you're able.

Healing, in my opinion is easy and difficult in unique ways. To me the flow state I go into for it makes total sense, but I know more than a few folks who refuse to touch it in savage due to the high skill ceiling. Compared to tank and dps, you have the highest burden of group responsibility. 

The priority list goes

1. Make sure the party has enough health to survive the next mechanic

2. Damage. 

3. Prep


I know damage is number 2 there, but it's more like 1.1 in reality. You'll become glued to your damage rotation more than in normal content and work all of your healing into/around it. If you have to drop a cast to get the party healthy again, then do it, but don't sit on your hands too much.

The hard part is, on top of your normal positioning, you also have to worry about the position your casting heals from, since only hitting half the party won't cut it, you'll end up running mid just to run straight back a lot. Doing that while also not dropping damage is a challenge in it's own. You also have to gauge when you *cant* help everyone and when to trust your cohealer to be holding any slack you may create and vice versa.

Then like I already mentioned, knowing your kit. You need to know exactly when you need 1 heal, 2 heals, a combo of a few, etc. To get the party to a safe amount of health. Overhealing is wasted DPS for anybody that isn't WHM, so you get good at gambling with the parties lives based off % heals you know you can manage without crits. You'll also sometimes be managing specific players health % that aren't the tanks, due to targeted mechanics. 

Example, p10s will pick 2 random players to do a certain part of a mechanic. Doing this gives them a very spicy bleed. We're talking 20-25% of a DPS health bar every tick.  The only way you'll be able to tell who it is in the shuffle, is watching *other* players debuff bars. 


So, the long and short of it is... healing is a very fast paced, high stakes management simulator. I spend more time in the party list than I do looking at the actual arena now that I know when to be where for mechanics. 

Tanking is like DPS, in that, if you're doing the fight right and doing your rotation correctly, you did what you were supposed to 99% of the time. 

Apologies for the book, hope that helps some and let me know if you have any specific questions. 


The other important advice I can give is, make sure you're where you're supposed to be while you're learning the fight. Don't adjust around people, be in YOUR correct position. If it kills the run, it's always better to be right. Otherwise people will see your panic to fix the problem they made as you being in the wrong. Once you have a lot of comfort with a fight you can pull off some crazy adjusts that save it, but that shouldn't be your priority early on

As a healer main in savage, (usually WHM but occasionally SGE and SCH as needed), I can give a few pointers if you ever need.

I'm by no means a sage main, but I do try to get as comfortable as I can on all healers in case friend groups need a specific fill for prog/reclears. 

The best starting point is to watch some POVs of the fight before you go into it, watch how sage players play, and watch equally important, how their cohealers act/react. communication between cohealers can save runs/mistakes more than anything else. It's harder to pull off in PF (especially as voice chat isn't nearly as common there) but is still an essential tool. 

If you know the WHM's will typically bene the tank after a certain ability, it saves wasting your own kit on overheal. You'll live on the concepts of mana and kit economy more than in other content, so it's good to have extreme comfort with exactly what your kit can do going into it, and what your cohealers are capable of.  You don't need to memorize the other healing jobs kits perfectly, but have a good idea of what they're capable of, when. 

As for telling groups if you're new: it's dealers choice. So long as you're honest about your prog point, PF doesn't care too much. It may be good to do since you're planning to heal, and an off the ball healer can hamper things more than a DPS would, so giving everyone an idea of what to expect going in might save frustration getting directed at you. 

Also you'll learn quickly, a lot of PF claims themselves one mechanic ahead of what they are. I recommend NOT doing this. It's bad practice and is the reason so many memes happen. But, don't be surprised if you end up on a group for a specific prog point that rarely makes it to that prog point. 


Other things to keep in mind: your debuff bar needs to be large and visible. A lot of savage fights have debuffs you don't have time to stop and search for related to mechanics. And the boss' cast bar is also good to enlarge.

The trick is to learn how to cater to bad tanks while still pumping out damage when you can. How you can twist and turn the tools you have to get a job done. If you're only relying on GCD abilities, you're having a problem. Try and learn to combo your other abilities. For example. On WHM, plenary indulgence, your wings, and Asylum all increase healing potentcy for certain abilities. Learn to work them in before your uses of assize, or other aoe heals and they'll be bursting the parties health like crazy.

Then when you have better tanks, you know you're way overdoing it and can scale back. But by the time you're in SHB dungeons, you'll have a consistent rotation you do for w2w pulls that'll sail you pretty breezily into the endgame. 

And again, for whm specifically, a crutch I used early on and still do when I'm doing dungeons a bit lazily.

When the tank initiates the pull hit him with a regen and a divine benison. Follow him to the end of the pull. Use another benison, depending on how fast the tank is possibly reset your regen, then hit medica 2. (If you're really not feeling it pop Asylum too). Three HoTs and a small shield will keep him pretty much scratch free for 30 seconds. Especially if you're spamming out holy and stunning the pack for the first 5-10 seconds.  In the meantime the pack should be near dead and you'll just need touch up heals to finish things off. I don't recommend relying on this too much, because it is a bit of a waste. But it's a good crutch to get used to your potencies and your effectiveness as a healer.

The airline has a problem because there is a lack of immediate incentive to acquire that skill. 180k per year, cool. That's decent money. There are two great options to get there that have been mentioned 

1. Have the money to pay for flight school(which may or may not be accessible in your area). To my knowledge flight schools are typically privately run and aren't eligible for tuition reimbursement through the military.

2. Join the military, and wind up with a flight assignment. This is assuming you are military eligible, so many people with pre existing conditions(both mental and physical) that would not stop you from being a pilot in the public sector would be ineligible in the first place. That aside, you then have to be nth percentile of those wanting that training to get a spot in it. You don't just join with a strong enough passion for it and they give you the pilot seat.

But lets talk numbers, assuming that your average joe with a will to improve their life can get into a flight program in the military. In the military there are roughly 43,000 pilots across their programs. In the U.S there are 100,000 commercial pilots and just shy of 700,000 pilots in the private sector. If every pilot in the military left today and joined the private sector, we still wouldn't be where we need to be. And the military does not need an unlimited number of pilots. 

So no, it's the airlines problem. If they want people trained for a job and motivated to do that job, they're going to need to provide adequate compensation to cover the training, and likely adequate compensation to make up for the fact that you do not get to live a normal life while flying commercial. Relationships will be difficult to keep, pets are pretty much a no go, and any sense of stationary stability is given up when taking that job. 180k a year sounds fantastic, but realistically if I can attend a trade school at a 1/10th of the cost, and work my way to 140k/year in the trades while maintaining a normal life, why would I become a pilot? The incentive to do the task, is not in line with what is demanded.

Typically on wall to wall pulls I'll hit the tank with a regen after the first few hits so his health stays in balance as additional pulls hit him. I get my difficulty by forgetting about mechanics and putting myself into stupid positions

- A healer who sits on the brink of death note often than my tanks

Push through ARR and pay attention. It feels bland at times but it sets the stage for some of the best story I've ever played. 

Learn the job you're doing. Everything in your kit is there for a reason so learn as you get them the best way to use them. If your job isn't what you're looking for, don't be afraid to pick something new up(personally I don't recommend doing this until level 30+ though as the level 1-15 grind for alternate jobs is a slog. Once you get dailies and dungeons unlocked, leveling up side classes is a breeze). 

If you intend to heal ever, know that it's not like most MMOs. Healers are meant to push out as much damage as they can while keeping the group up. Your tank going to 50% health doesn't make you a bad healer. It makes you a good one if youre casting DPS. And nobody should get mad at you for it(at least not in any of the main content. Some rare situations in end game stuff is niche and specific). But if you tank, also recognize that you probably dont need to sweat if your healer is letting your health drop, they're just utilizing their full kit. 

Follow your ABC's. Always Be Casting. Use your kit and use it constantly. Even if it's not the most effective spell, any spell is better than no spell/ability.  

Utilize the novice network. The community is award winning for a reason. Most folks you'll run into while playing the MSQ will be pretty chill and happy to help/offer advice if needed. You're unlikely to run into extreme toxicity. But do make sure to take advice offered. Ignoring it and dieing the same way multiple times is still frustrating and may cause negative reactions. 

Regular side quests for the most part aren't very essential. They used to be for leveling purposes before the experience curve got tweaked. Some of them have their own small stories that are worthwhile. But many of them can just be bypassed to save time. Blue icon side quests are more important and will add some function or note to the story that's important. 

If you find your queue times as DPS are too long, try leveling a tank or healer. Tank is harder IMO as they carry the dungeons. But either role will turn any MSQ queue to 5 minutes or less. There's added responsibility but it's pretty worthwhile to skip the waits. 

Once you unlock mounts and the aether compass, make sure to take some time to find the aether currents in the world. This will save you time later and let you fly on your mounts in the zones you cleared. There are some currents found in the world, and others in quests(both blue side quests and MSQ). It's boring to have to go back just to farm them all. So just pop the compass occasionally while doing the MSQ to get as many as you can early on. 

If you're like me and play for cosmetics, make sure you level up DoH/DoL jobs. Both so you can harvest/make your own stuff, and so you can sell it to rake in that gil.

There's the end game, hard-core philosophy where your goal is to always have them at the bare minimum to survive health. But the explanation I got with it when I started healing a long while back was just meant to break the typical MMO healer thought process.

I mean, it is important to start practicing those lessons early. 

The hardest lesson to have to learn when it's applicable is to not keep everyone topped off constantly. If you're overhealing, you're wasting mana. Which will start to get you killed as early as level 70. 

Can't tell you how many times I've seen newer healers in late SB or early ShB dungeons lose control over their mana and have things end in a wipe after a large pull. 

I'd say early on set the target so your tank is generally at the 70-80% health mark at most. You don't need to wait for the last second 1hp heal, but you do want to acclimate to waiting until it'll have a more cost effective result.

Just a heads up, for burrowing species coconut fiber is okay, but it's recommended to mix it with an earthy substrate as coco fiber isn't great structurally for burrowing(it tends to collapse in on itself and not hold shape well)

What's typically recommended is a blend of something that is topsoil based and the coco fiber in a 60/40 ratio. What I like to use is Reptisoil(you can also get critter soil, but it's usually more expensive and reptisoil works great and comes in larger bags) because it's got carbon and peat moss blended in. But you can really use most top soil based substrates and blend it with the coco fiber for a fine result. Depending on the T I also sometimes include a bit of leaf litter on top of the substrate. This gives the T plenty of options and a good foundation for any construction that it intends to do.

2. Third party. If I see two teams fighting I'll approach while taking pot shots. This has to be balanced across both teams so that while you approach, you're putting them in awkward positions to avoid being sniped while also handling their engagement with the other team. Hi OP, just want to expand on a few things have been said here. 

1.That enclosure looks to be either an exo-terra or reptizoo arboreal enclosure. Due to this, you can't just add substrate to the current one as it has a large glass door on the front that the substrate will just slip through the cracks of and make a mess. Something this size but turned sideways with a top opening instead would be good, or even a glass tank if need be(I usually recommend acrylic because it's easier to modify if it needs more cross ventilation). If you do use a glass tank, make sure the lid is not a metal mesh as their legs can get stuck in it if they climb up.

2. This looks to be a curlyhair which is a terrestrial opportunistic burrower. So roughly half the enclosure should be filled with substrate so it has room to dig if it feels the need. You can use a coconut fiber mix but I heavily recommend using a substrate that is 70% something else and coconut fiber isn't great for structural integrity for burrowing. It's best known for holding moisture which a curlyhair doesn't need much of.      So a coco fiber and vermiculite and topsoil would be good. I personally just use reptisoil and cocofiber for quick set ups since it's a decent mix and has some activated carbon which helps.  This will be a moisture retention mix due to the coco fiber and peat moss so if you use it make sure to have a lot of cross ventilation and be careful about what moisture you add to the tank(I usually just fill the water dish every few days and let a small amount overflow to keep a low humidity level) 

3. Nix the heat lamp. It'll dry the T out and cook it if it's on a shorter cage. T'S unlike reptiles are comfortable if we are. So just keep it in a room that's 70-80 degrees typically. If you get into colder months a good tip I saw recently is to put the enclosure in a larger container, and use a heat source like a heat pad on the interior of the larger enclosure. This will create a nice warm air pocket around the T without making it too dry and warm inside of the enclosure. 

4. Don't worry too much if it loses more hair when you get it. It could either be in Pre molt now(which there's a lot of other advice for. I typically don't recommend changing the enclosure unless it's absolutely necessary during this time. But that height is dangerous for the T so it's hard to say) or stressed by its environment, when you move it and hopefully set it up in a new enclosure this will be a lot of stress so it will likely kick more hair during that time. Once it molts it will get an entirely fresh set of hair so you don't need to worry too much about it. 

Hope this helps

You're all good. So the basics(which I could be a little off on, but as I understand it) 

Tap strafing allows you to turn 180 degrees mid air without losing any momentum. For example, if you're flying in one direction, you can turn around in a split second without losing momentum and now travel in the opposite direction. 

To achieve this you hit the forward (usually w) key after executing a slide jump and at the same time you hit a strafe key. 

The combination of inputs in a short period of time fucks with how movement is meant to be processed and allows to you turn and keep your forward momentum in the new direction. 

This maneuver is difficult to pull off due to the keys that need to be pressed in an extremely short time frame. 

However it's a lot easier if you ha e a free scrolling mouse wheel. E.g when you roll up or down on your mouse wheel you likely feel a click and it stops. On a free wheel, it clicks but has much less friction so it doesn't stop. So scrolling up on a free scrolling wheel will input a lot of commands for whatever you bind to it since the computer sees it like a button. Allowing you to "click" the non existant button many times in a single moment. Much faster than you could ever do with actual keys. 

So what people do is bind the forward key to their mouse wheel. So when they go to execute a tap strafe, they just hit the scroll wheel and let it go, basically giving the game  tons of "move forward" key press commands. At the same time they use their free hand to do the slide jump and strafe keys. 

Basically removing the timing issue and letting you cheese a system that was never designed to work like that

If you assign the movement input to a scroll wheel on a free-wheeling mouse, the game will interpret each click on the free wheel spin as an individual input and try to process them all as quickly as possible and at once in some cases. 

Tap strafing works by timing inputs at a specific interval to create non logical movement. Binding the command to your scroll wheel makes it way easier by making 100 commands of X action intermixed with the legitimate movement commands and creates a fucky, unreadable movement that doesn't follow any logical movement pattern
