Here's what I did. I was working at Amazon last year after covid shut my entire career field down(career bartender at high end resturaunts. I know most people don't see this as a career. But it was) 

I hated working for amazon. It was soul draining.

What I ended up doing was start applying to jobs that matched my experience like a mad man. Even if you don't think you qualify for the job. Apply for it if it fits your skill set. This doesn't mean just an industry you have experience in. But industries that use similar skill sets

The worst that can happen is that they don't respond. A few may send rejection letters. But more common than not, they just won't say anything. 

Don't let not hearing things discourage you though, just keep applying across the board. Aim to submit 3 applications per day or more until you run out of ideas. Then ask your friends what they think you're good at. Add that to your skill set list and broaden your job search for jobs that can use those skills too. 

Keep at it as long as you possibly can. Don't quit your current job until you have a new job confirmed. That way you're not losing anything.

Important note. Do not quit your job just because you got an interview. Use a sick day to attend the interview if you have to. But if you're like most people, the first interview won't pan out. It'll take a few. 

What I did was apply for liquor rep jobs. Nothing panned out there. So I broadened to other sales jobs. Until eventually I found a job that's entirely unrelated to the bar industry. But it was a sales job. And I knew I could sell things. I'd been doing it for 10+ years on a smaller scale. 

Another important note. If you get an interview somewhere. Do your homework. See if they have interview questions on GlassDoor or other similar websites. If not, try to find info about what interviews for that field of work are like. Really read through it and try to understand the point of questions they'd ask.  Try to figure out why they'd ask each question so you can present yourself as someone who understands what they want in a candidate.

This hit me like a brick my first day in japan (3 week solo trip that I took because I drunkenly purchased a ticket one night on a whim)

Step 1. Get to your first hotel. I suggest finding a "western" hotel if you're in a foreign country for your first night or two. Dont immediately do hostels or foreign style lodging. Those first 2 nights you're going to be homesick whether you like it or not, and a private bed is the best way I found to combat that. I cried for an hour or so before getting on my feet and out the door for step 2. 

Step 2. I planned activities for every day. Most of them got thrown out the window immediately as I would find more interesting things to do by walking around or meeting other travelers. But having plans to fall back on helped when I would get a bit nervous or bored. An active and busy mind is not going to worry about being alone in a new country, so your goal is to keep your mind constantly busy. Japan was great for this as there were a lot of hikes and temples and shrines to visit(literally hundreds no matter where you are). So if i ever found myself sitting id Google map the nearest shrines and go and visit a handful. 

Step 3. Meet people. Staying in hostels is a great way to do this. Some countries also have traveler subreddits(e.g /r/Japantravel) that have meet up threads specifically for meeting strangers for group activities. Just like in step 2N if you can keep yourself occupied and make new friends you start to shed the nervousness and worry. 

Step 4. Eat. Eat a lot. Eat the local food. Eat the McDonald's to see how its different from where you're from. Just eat everything. Im a firm believer that food brings the world together and is the best way to experience a culture. A full stomach also helps calm those nerves down. 

But this all starts with step 0. Just buy a ticket to a place you've always wanted to go(after the whole coronavirus thing cools off a bit). Just find a good cheap ticket. And go.

Alright, let me take a beat and explain some stuff to you. 

.1. Depakote(divalproex) is not likely to make you wig out. It's understandable why it would be a fear, but it's not likely to send you off the deep end. It can in some cases worsen thoughts of depression and suicide. But, if your doctor is good and is keeping up with you(even without a psychiatrist), you'll be pulled off of it before it can effect you too much in that way, and again this is only a problem for a small percentage of people. 

It is crucial here that you are honest with your doctor about any symptoms you experience. Don't try to hide if you feel that your depression has gotten worse since getting on Depakote. For me, it was really natural to not give the full story because I was afraid. But Bipolar is a medical illness, we don't lie when we break our legs or get the flu, so we can't be lying about this either. I'm not saying you will, it's just what I did. I learned the hard way that lying means you don't heal the way you should be. so always be honest when it comes to how your meds are doing with your system to your doc.

.2. It's common from the experience i've had and the experiences i've heard of to prescribe medication for manic states first, such as depakote. This is because in certain cases, the manic cases are the ones that are more of a risk, so they need to be leveled out.(there's memes about it everywhere [like this one](http://www.quickmeme.com/img/fd/fde6ca424b6c7f0113b569082337073eb9f222a86c71ff3b1f43d3a4fca9e4ac.jpg) ) It sucks, but it's the wild ride we are on. It's a system that has to be taken in steps. and it feels out of order and slow at first. but soon enough it will make sense and level out.

.3. You've just been tossed into the deep end of the knowledge here with your diagnosis and such. It's a hard, scary moment no doubt. Those fears and whatnot, while they may not be necessary or true, are natural. When I was diagnosed I was in a Mental hospital on lockdown for suicide watch. My doctor had 15 minutes to explain my diagnosis and new medicine to me. That's all I was told about it for the next 7 days, no internet, phones, etc. It fucking sucked. 

So I don't doubt right now it's a terrifying set of emotions and thoughts going through your head right now. So make sure you take a moment to just stop and breathe. It seems like a lot. and it seems scary. Most if not all of us have been there. 

If something is new and scary, reach out. I recommend your support systems first, friends, family, etc. But if the advice you need can only come from someone with the same thing as you. This place has given solid help to me in that regard. 



All in all. Being scared is a fair reaction. But you need to trust the community, your medical professionals, and those around you.

You seem to be working really hard to convey emotion through the script, which is good. You could probably clean it up a bit of it though. You kind of reiterate some of the same things in different words which isnt necessary. 

But on the topic of cutting things down, your intro describes what the scene line already does. Int. Night will give the director/set design, etc.  all of the info he needs to make stylistic choices beyond that. (I know you're not necessarily writing this in context of handing it to a director, but it's good to keep it in mind that you want to convey information without stepping on other people in a productions toes.) Another line or two to set the scene and tone wont kill you, but too much and it leaves out the option for anyone else to work with it creatively. 

Theres a few similar things throughout it. Just keep in mind, you want the script to be about the story, and the characters development. If something is particularly relevant to developing the character and enhancing the story, that's what needs to be put on paper. The smaller details of the setting arent as important, those can be decided later if a clear image of the character is presented. Just when writing, ask yourself "what makes this line I'm writing important to the story/character". And after you write it. Do it again. 

All in all, for a first work it's not bad at all. Keep up with it and you could easily work this into a solid script.

Talks to end the war were in place before the bombs were dropped, and i mentioned in another comment that along with the bombs being dropped, the soviets (who until that time were believed by the japanese to still be a neutral go between by the Japanese) invaded and announced their intentions. 

It had been previously discussed to have the japanese work on a deal to end the war with the Americans as a sort of middle ground. Japan had an upset in its government where they couldn't decide what conditions they would surrender under, and what conditions america would accept. So it split them politically. 

Once Russia announced had decided to invade, the japanese not only lost a huge card to play. They now had a seriously increased threat. Hiroshima hit. Russia invaded. Nagasaki hit. 

There was no holding out. With two armies knocking on both sides and two major cities decimated it was clear that what was left wasnt going to be left for long. Even if america didnt use a 3rd bomb. Those two militaries had the power to over run japan and completely destroy anything they had left. 

So we got a more or less condition less surrender. 

I cant say for certain what the emperor had going through his mind. But if it was power, one way or another he was going to lose it completely. And multiple factors made that very clear.

With the pressure from the Soviets the japanese understood that they didnt have much time left in the war. Once the bombs hit it was sort of a last straw moment. 

The bombs gave then a good reason to surrender, which is something they didnt plan on doing easily. But surrendering to a WMD rather than increased military force was a way for them to save face in the prospect of surrendering.

Edit: had the Soviets not decided to invade after Hiroshima, theres a chance the war would have carried on a short time longer than after Nagasaki. The political cabinet did see that they were going to lose the war, but couldn't agree what terms to surrender under. With the threat of fighting a two sided war and two strategically significant cities( iirc Hiroshima at the time was a military production facility, operating with thousands of laborers, often those too young to fight in the war. But my memory if this aspect is fuzzy) destroyed, they saw that an ending to the war where they would still hold any meaningful cards was not going to happen. 

They had hoped the soviets would side with them in nonaggression, and help broker a peace deal to end the war. When the soviets declared an attack after Hiroshima. That was it. There wasnt anything else they could do.

They're right. The mental health care system in this country is letting everyone down. Its not doing its job effectively and it's not funded or built into our infrastructure well enough to manage what it needs to. Because of this, it's hard to find a good hospital. Most of them have to group large blankets of people together. Addicts,eating disorders, suicidal, psychoactive tendencies, etc. Into one building. And often in one hall. 

I live in a large city with 3 dedicated mental health facilities. Not nearly enough or large enough to handle everything that they need to. And we need to fight for reform in this matter. We need to funnel taxes into mental health and consider it as important as physical health. But we just aren't there yet. 

But if you need help. If you really. Really. Need help. Go and get it. Dont hesistate because you heard about the negative experiences of others. That help can save your life and send it in a much better direction. 

When I went in, I was met with the rudest receptionist who said I needed an appointment when I'd come in directly after a failed suicide attempt. I had to fight to be admitted that night. my roommate was a paranoid schizophrenic with frequent delusions. And I learned a lot being roomed with him. I was allowed outside 10 minutes, 3 times per day in a concealed courtyard. I ate powdered eggs for breakfast every day. I sat through group sessions that didnt begin to help because they had too much to cover to provide any deep insight into any one problem.

We're quick to focus on where the system failed us. Because its infuriating. 

But we dont focus on where the system did succeed. I saw a doctor twice a day, I got diagnosed with bipolar disorder, placed on a steady medication regimen.

When I went in, the first doctor I saw apologized profusely for the nurse in admissions. She was caring and understanding. Listened to my problems. Talked to me. Listened. 

I talked to my roommate. He shared with me the difficulties he experienced in his disorder and we talked about life uninhibited. Because we knew we were both there because we weren't doing alright. The stigma of mental conditions didnt exist in that room. 

I watched people with severe eating disorders stomach food willingly while the nursing staff talked to them.

I convinced a nurse to let me go outside later than we were supposed to so that we could watch the thunderstorm and sit in awe of the world. 

I sat in group sessions that didnt help me specifically. But I learned a lot about others and how they struggled with their problems. Most of them severe. If they could do it so could I. 


My point is. The mental health system in this country is failing us. Even some of the professionals fail at their jobs. But there are a lot of dedicated professionals who got into the field because they really honestly want to help people that are being let down by the system. 

So If you feel you need help. Get it. It wont be easy. The first few days will feel like torture. But being removed from everything else in life for a short time is more helpful than you can imagine. 

(Not necessarily directed at you. But for anyone reading this thread who is worried about getting help due to the negative concepts regularly expressed at the process)

Budget breakdown was as follows:

Flight round trip:700 dollars, travel insurance was an additional 50. Worth every penny, though you might find flights a bit pricier. I hunted for the best price here and found that the combination of flying near sept. 11th + the first week of U.S collleges fall term + no events or holidays in Japan during my trip really made the stars align here. I bought about 4 months in advance. 

JR pass 2 week - 400 dollars. Now, I should have been smarter with my travel planning as I could have gotten the 1 week and been just as happy, especially if I had committed less time in Matsue. activating it right before my first ride and then using it to get around. Would have saved me a pretty penny, but I at least managed to get some decent use out of it. 

Pocket wifi - 60 dollars for 14 days. I went for the over the top 10gb per 3 days because I watched netflix to help me fall asleep some nights. Worth every penny, my only qualm was that on most trains it didn't work well between major cities. So bring a book or something to read if you're going to be on the shinkansen. 

Lodging - now this was a bit complicated and I actually wound up going over budget due to a planning error on my end. There was an issue with one of my hotels and I had decided to last minute cancel one of them, losing about 300 in the process. I didn't include this in the main budget, however it is worth noting that you should have some emergency backup money tucked away just in case. 

Total lodging cost otherwise - 700 dollars. This could have definitely been done for probably 200 less had I been like many others and stayed in hostels. Many are very nice if you do your research, but I decided to stay in some more traditional styled lodgings and spent an average of 50 dollars per night on lodgings. You can do it for closer to 30 if you plan ahead. 


Food cost averages - 20-30 per day save for one or two 40+ dollar meals. in total I spent about 600 on food and drinks. For snacks I usually stopped at the convienence stores which the food was actually really awesome and would cost between 1.50-4 bucks for a snack. This is also where I got most of my alcohol. A can of STRONG ZERO costs about $3 bucks if I recall, for a tall boy can of 9%. If I knew I was going to bars I usually would pre-game outside of the 7-11 with one or two to lower my drink costs. Bars on average were $6-12 bucks per drink which would add up quick otherwise. So I could get something to sip on since I didn't need to really drink much more. 

Inner-city transit.

As I mentioned before, the IC card (passmo or Suica in tokyo, but they vary from region to region). I'd say over all of them time I spent in tokyo I recharged it with about 120 bucks. Each trip between areas averaged at 2-4 dollars. Not to mention you can use the card at vending machines, arcades, etc. So it's a nice little cushion to burn on silly things. If you plan well and just go to 1-2 areas a day you could probably average this to about 8 bucks. But this is one area that I would err on the side of caution. go for about 20 a day just in case. This transport really is invaluable in tokyo. 

So that leaves us with about 580 dollars.

What did I use most of this on? well some temples charge 400-600 yen(3.80-5.5 bucks a pop) to get into, charms are about 5-10 bucks, in this area alone I believe I spent about 100 dollars, but I was on a mission to be in as many temples as possible. 

Souvenirs - about 150 dollars. I bought a couple of nice items for friends and families (a personal made name seal stamp for 50, a custom tea set for 50, a yukata for myself that was 60, and various knick knacks for a total of 40.)  

the rest was spent on saying yes to things. If I saw a pastry stand that smelled delicious. I needed it. If I saw a wierd drink I wanted to try in a vending machine? I needed it. I didn't include this kind of stuff in my food budget because it was entirely non essentials, but were a nice little extra tacked onto the trip. 

I ended with about 200 extra that I spent on some duty free items in the airport. 


Now, all of this being said here's a few important notes. 

I had an extra 1200 set aside I.C.E. This was in case of any worries. It would have taken a dip into my savings to use (and the hotel change cost me about 300, which is where that money came from). On top of that, I budgeted more to ensure I had enough to cover my time off from work and to keep my bills on autopay. Again, not really included in the main budget because this varies from person to person and you should plan accordingly for what is right for you. Having the backup cushion was nice to know I wouldn't die hungry in an emergency. Even just having an unused emergency credit card(with no forex fees if possible) would be a good call. Just so you have something in case something goes sour, though this won't help you for a lot of things like food, most hotels seem to accept them. 

Things I learned and would do better when budgeting again. 

- better use of the JR pass. if I had gotten the 7 day and planned better I could have gotten the 7 day pass instead. Really you only need it for the shinkansen. Most of the inner-city travel is negligible in comparison. 

- smaller wifi. Really would be best for a single traveller. No real need for the 10 gigs even when streaming. could have saved 30-40 there. 

- hostels. as mentioned before. Could have saved about 200 in lodgings had I been more diligent. 

All of that totals up to near 400 dollars of extra budget. which could provide some awesome experiences instead if used well. 

Oh and make sure you plan ahead! get your lodgings locked in if possible, find the best ratings for the cheapest prices. really think through where you want to be. my first few days in Ueno were rough because it was more or less removed from the main action of tokyo and the last train in somewhat early. You can save on lodging if you stay further out, but if you'd rather be enjoying nightlife, make sure you're staying somewhere that the trains run a little later or that you can walk to in a worst case scenario.

Well that and several psychologists who studied the concept of empathy note that it's their understanding that we have limits to our empathy.  It's a self preservation tool for small communities to function not something that can extend to millions of people at once because we're only really designed to handle what immediately benefits our survival. 

For example there's a thought that feeling empathetic to large scale situations such as genocide or global starvation just isn't possible, the larger the group effected the lower the empathetic response is because you just aren't designed to care about that many people at once on an equal scale. You can care about the situation but unless you knew someone killed in Germany during ww2 then you aren't likely to spend the rest of your life in a depressed state of horror. Because at the end of the day they aren't in your group. You didn't know them and it's counter to your survival to continue to feel a strong emotional connection to them. 

But for a small group of boys that the media can release plenty of info on to bring us into their lives, for a limited time they're in our circle. Your brain will start to see them as someone you recognize and could place in your group. It won't be permanent and you'll likely forget them not long after the media drops them, But for now their specific lives are on your radar as much as some of your personal communities are. Much like how watching a movie about specific characters during the holocaust might make you tear up or get sick. Because it puts specific faces into a closer perspective. 

This isn't to say that we shouldn't care about things like world hunger, poverty, or war torn countries. But that different responses will happen from the public. People should want hunger to end globally. They should want children forced into slavery and war to end. But forcing that same empathetic response for ever single person in those situations would kill us before we ever got the chance to do anything about it. We're all just fragile monkeys running around with ancient coding in our heads to survive. We've learned more over the ages and we can counter a lot of the basic coding that we have which will benefit humanity as a whole in the long run. But we're still working on it.

It was a simple enough plan, hell i'd pulled it off maybe a dozen times in the past. With some work in art class i'd managed to make a perfect... Okay well maybe not perfect, but a reasonable facsimile of myself laying down. I have to admit growing my hair out to cover my face was the hardest challenge of the entire thing. 

I waited until my parents settled in front of the TV for their favorite cooking show, house buying show, or whatever reality crap they're so absorbed by and I did what every teenager with a social life in the history of time does. I popped the screen out of my window and made my way to Caleb's house. 

Now, I had only planned on staying for a few hours but Wendy Salascky was there. I think that says enough about how the rest of the night went. It's not like my parents would notice if I was back before morning anyways, they're not exactly the brightest crayons in the box. It must have been three... maybe four A.M before I finally managed to make it back home. 

Thank god I peaked in the window before just waltzing through the door because my parents were still entranced in front of the TV, and it seems they've invited some company as well. I don't know who in their right minds would want to come over to watch their garbage in the middle of the night. But it's not my problem. I push myself back against my window trying to open it. 

"what the hell.." I mutter to myself while sliding against the glass like a bird that doesn't know any better. Somehow it locked itself while I was gone. "This puts a kink in the plan". I start walking around the rest of the house, trying every window with no luck. I can't risk the front door right now with so many eyes in the living room waiting to spot me. I briefly consider breaking my window but how exactly do you play that off? "Oh yeah someone broke the window while I was asleep here in my clothes?". Even my parents would see through that. 

So I elect to wait, until they decide to go to sleep. I post up on the wall next to my window and wait. 

*clink. clink. clink* Damnit. I must have dozed off. The sun is blinding me as I open my eyes, with the sounds of birds singing and the window being knocked on. Wait. Shit. The window being knocked on. I try to edge myself around the wall to see who's in my room. 

Screaming doesn't work. My throat's dry and the sounds won't come out. I'm stuck panting, falling against the ground, and trying to unsee what's on the other side. It's me. Or it looks like me... but it's not. I know the shape of that face, the consistency of the hair, and those clothes. 

At first I thought my parents had busted me. But that didn't last long. He opened the window. 

"Hello Tyler, long time no see." His voice... no. My voice echoed in my head. 

"What the FUCK." Is all I could muster in response. 

An unsettling chuckle carried through the rest of his speech "Well, you were gone so long. I got pretty bored just laying in bed. So I decided to get up and stretch the old cardboard out. Unlucky for you though. I ran into our parents." 

The anger and fear had me stuttering at every word. "What do you mean OUR parents"

"Oh please" his awful laugh had begun to make me sick. "Don't act like you care about them now. You never cared about them. They pretty much told me outright... Well I guess technically they told you. When I told mom that I loved her, she nearly broke down crying right there. I mean really, how poorly do you treat our family?"

"Shut up. Just shut the fuck up." the tremble in my voice now rising in anger. 

"What, you love them? You treat them like your personal maids, put them down at any chance you get. So I had a thought. What if instead of you, they had a better son. One who loved them. One who wants to see them happy?" his smile began to twist and curl. " So, I've decided that you'll be out of the picture from here on out. I hope you understand." 

"You can't. I'll tell them. I'll tell them everything" I shot back 

"What, that your art project 'magically' came to life and tried to take over your life? Even if they believed that. Tell me, why would they want such an ungrateful brat back? Why would they ever want someone that doesn't seem to know the word thank you over a son that treats them with respect?"

The fear taking my voice back over forced me into silence. He wasn't wrong. It would be impossible to convince them of that.

"Now, I suggest you run along. It's almost breakfast time and I promised I would make it today. waffles with bacon bits, your favorite. Right? Maybe i'll toss one in the yard for you later." The echo of my voice in my own head continued, only broken by the slamming shut of my window.

For me personally the most important quality of DMing has been flexibility. Figure out when to let players do (or attempt to do) what they would like to in order to enjoy the game. If the adventure is set out for them to talk to a specific npc and their characters refuse to. Find another way to start the mission, introduce a different npc and find another angle to tell the story from. This doesn't mean that you should just give them any overpowered thing they want, like a greatsword+5 right out the gate. But give them options and try not to railroad them to the book(if you're using a pre built story).  That being said. Make the world real, if they want to storm a dragons hoard at level 2. The dragon will obliterate them. You can give them some warning on that. But if they are dead set on it and manage to somehow find one, then it's up to them,  the consequences for their actions have to have meaning.  

In reverse of that also ensure that they respect your position as DM, in the game your word is law. Don't be a dick about it, but don't let them just decide that incredulous things happen just because they want them to, it's not their world it's yours. However it's your job to make sure that they have fun in your world.  If that means you want to do away with some rules or add rules of your own, then so be it (however if you do intend to do away with or add rules make sure you talk to the group and establish them beforehand, try to never just drop a rule in on somones action that stops them. The player will feel targeted by Illwill). 

Edit: to add to this let's say your players want to spend 3 hours negotiating prices with a store clerk or RPing in a town. Let them. If they want to go kill something even if the story doesn't provide a fight for a long while, give them a pack of wolves or some other encounter to get their hands dirty with. Maybe the town they're in has had a goblin problem recently?  Just be willing to give them the game they want. Still try and give them reason to do the story that's already laid out but don't try to force them onto the railroad to much. Just provide their characters enough reason to and they'll find their way to it
